core1a.prerequisites: Kinetic energy is one half mass times speed squared; force times distance has units of joules.
core1a.core: Separate the energy ledger from momentum conservation.
core1a.guide: The teacher anchors the model using a simple 2 kg cart with adjustable surface resistance.
core1a.wrong: Do not conserve momentum during external friction.
core1a.conditions: Constant friction requires a controlled patch; measurements of only distance establish average work.
core1a.question: How do speed and resistance change stopping distance?
guideSteps: Define the cart and the braking surface.
Identify normal force, gravity and friction directions.
Use one-half mass times speed squared.
Express friction work as force times displacement.
Higher speed requires more work; zero resistance means no finite stopping distance.

A.reasoning_demand: Separate force balance from stopping work on one uniform surface
A.prediction: If kinetic friction doubles at fixed entry speed, what happens to stopping distance?
A.challenge: Synthetic: A 2 kg toy cart enters a horizontal rough patch at 4 m/s. The constant friction force is 4 N. Predict and calculate the stopping distance without treating friction as additional kinetic energy.

fields.label: Choose the energy model
choices: Initial kinetic energy is removed by friction work
Momentum is conserved as the cart stops
fields.expected: Initial kinetic energy is removed by friction work
fields.mistake: Friction is an external force that does negative work

fields.label: Stopping distance (m)
fields.mistake: Initial K = 16 J and friction is 4 N, so distance = 4 m

fields.label: Explain the work–energy balance and units

hints: Decide which force acts along the displacement and what sign its work has.
Set magnitude of friction work equal to the initial kinetic energy only after identifying the system.
worked: The cart loses kinetic energy to the rough surface; momentum is not constant.
The 4 N friction force removes 4 J per metre, so 4d = 16 J and d = 4 m.
A.boundary: Boundary test: the same cart enters the same patch at 8 m/s with the same constant friction force. Is the stopping distance still 4 m?

boundaryFields.label: Choose the speed dependence
choices: Stopping distance scales with the square of speed
boundaryFields.expected: Stopping distance scales with the square of speed
boundaryFields.mistake: At fixed force, energy is proportional to speed squared

boundaryFields.label: Changed distance (m)
boundaryFields.mistake: Speed doubling multiplies kinetic energy by four

boundaryFields.label: Explain why speed doubling changes distance by this factor

A.boundaryCheck: At 8 m/s the cart has 64 J. The same 4 N friction takes 16 m to stop.

B.reasoning_demand: Infer friction from measured stopping distance and test whether constant friction remains justified
B.prediction: If a cart stops over 2 m from the same entry speed, what could that say about the average friction force?
B.challenge: Synthetic unfamiliar setting: A rolling test cart of mass 2 kg enters an unknown coating at 4 m/s and stops over a measured 2 m. Assume other losses are negligible. Infer its average resistive force, then state what extra measurements you need before claiming friction is constant.

fields.label: Choose the inference model
choices: Infer average resistance from measured work
fields.expected: Infer average resistance from measured work
fields.mistake: Only net work and displacement determine an average force, not its time profile

fields.label: Inferred mean resistive force (N)
fields.mistake: 16 J dissipated over 2 m means mean force = 8 N

fields.label: Explain what is and is not determined by stopping distance

hints: First compute energy lost rather than assuming the friction value from Task A.
Only the integral of force over distance is fixed by a stopping measurement; an exact force-versus-position profile is not.
worked: As before, K = 16 J at entry and zero at rest.
Mean F along travel is 16 J / 2 m = 8 N opposing motion.
This does not prove the force was constantly 8 N; different force–distance profiles could have the same work.
B.boundary: Boundary test: measured force becomes linearly larger with position across a 2 m patch but its average remains 8 N. Can the original stopping-distance measurement alone reconstruct that force profile?

boundaryFields.label: Choose the data-identification claim
choices: No, one work integral cannot determine a unique force profile
Yes, all forces must be constant at 8 N
boundaryFields.expected: No, one work integral cannot determine a unique force profile
boundaryFields.mistake: An integral of force does not identify its shape

B.boundaryCheck: The same mean force gives the same total work over 2 m; time- or position-resolved measurements are needed to recover a unique profile.
